# Suppārakajātaka (Ja 463)
**ID:** Ja 463
**Section:** Jātaka (ja)
**Collection:** Suttas-Late-1
**Title (Pali):** Suppārakajātaka
**SuttaCentral:** https://suttacentral.net/ja463
**tipitaka.org (CST):** https://tipitaka.org/romn/cscd/s0513m.mul10.xml

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature and SuttaCentral)
*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and SuttaCentral data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*
The *Suppārakajātaka* (Jātaka No. 463) is the ninth story in the *Ekādasanipāta* of the Pali Jātaka collection [Fausböll 1887]. Delivered by the Buddha while staying at Jetavana, the discourse is framed around the Master's extraordinary wisdom and perfection of knowledge (*mahāpaññā*) [SuttaCentral; Fausböll 1887; Pye].
The narrative relates a past life in which the Bodhisatta was born as Suppāraka (Suppārakapaṇḍita), a wise and skilled master mariner residing at the port of Bharukaccha [Fausböll 1887; Speyer 1895; Pye]. Although Suppāraka had become blind from his years of seafaring, merchants bound on an ocean expedition beseech him to serve as their chief steersman, trusting that no vessel guided by him ever meets with disaster [Winternitz 1933; Fausböll 1887; Speyer 1895]. During their voyage—viewed by modern scholars as reflecting maritime routes between Bharukaccha and regions such as Suvaṇṇabhūmi [Hazra 1982; Ray 1946]—the vessel goes astray in dangerous and wondrous seas. Guided by Suppāraka's mariners' lore, the crew navigates through the *Khuramāla* ocean, where fish-like creatures with human forms and razor-sharp snouts plunge in and out of the water, followed by the glowing *Aggimāla* ocean yielding gold, and the curd-like *Dadhimāla* ocean yielding silver [Barua 1921; Readings from the Jatakas].
Text-reuse analysis by DharmaNexus records comprehensive overlap between the core verses and the *Jātaka-aṭṭhakathā* [DharmaNexus]. Outside Pali literature, the legend corresponds closely to the *Supāragajātaka* in Āryaśūra's Sanskrit *Jātakamālā*, a parallel highlighted in comparative studies and corroborated by substantial cross-language text reuse matches identified by DharmaNexus [Speyer 1895; DharmaNexus]. DharmaNexus further registers cross-language alignments with Tibetan canonical literature, including sections of the *Mahāvyutpatti* [DharmaNexus].

- Text reuse within the Pali corpus (DharmaNexus): Jātaka-aṭṭhakathā (Catuttho bhāgo) (Atk S0513a4) (§4.4–6.4 ↔ §1343_2–1351)
- Cross-language matches (DharmaNexus): Āryaśūra: Jātakamālā (SA_T09_bsa032) [sa]; Āryaśūra: Jātakamālā (SA_T09_ajm_u) [sa]; བྱེ་བྲག་ཏུ་རྟོགས་པར་བྱེད་པ། ([vyutpatti]) (D4346) [bo]; BO_K01_D0003-4_H0003-4 [bo]
**Sources**

- [SuttaCentral] SuttaCentral record for ja463 — Title, English title, framing setting at Jetavana on the perfection of knowledge.
- [DharmaNexus] DharmaNexus database — Pali-internal text reuse with Jātaka-aṭṭhakathā and cross-language alignments with Āryaśūra's Jātakamālā and Tibetan texts.
- [Fausböll 1887] V. Fausböll, Jātaka Together with Its Commentary, Vol. 4 (1887) — Pali text, location in the Ekādasanipāta, Bharukaccha setting, and dialogue regarding Suppāraka's blindness.
- [Winternitz 1933] Maurice Winternitz, A History of Indian Literature, Vol. 2 (1933) — Characterization of the story as a mariners' fairy tale of clever blind Suppāraka.
- [Hazra 1982] Kanai Lal Hazra, History of Theravāda Buddhism in South-East Asia (1982) — Connection of the narrative to voyages between Bharukaccha and Suvaṇṇabhūmi.
- [Ray 1946] Niharranjan Ray, An Introduction to the Study of Theravāda Buddhism in Burma (1946) — Discussion of Bharukaccha and Suvaṇṇabhūmi maritime commerce.
- [Speyer 1895] J. S. Speyer (tr.), The Jātakamālā: Garland of Birth-Stories of Āryaśūra (1895) — Comparison between the Sanskrit Jātakamālā account of Supāraga and the Pali Suppāraka redaction.
- [Barua 1921] Benimadhab Barua, Prakrit Dhammapada (1921) — Citation of verse phrase describing beings plunging in and out of the water.
- [Pye] Michael Pye, Skilful Means: A Concept in Mahayana Buddhism — Analysis of the Bodhisatta as wise and skilled in means.
- [Readings from the Jatakas] Readings from the Jatakas — English translation and verses describing the Khuramāla, Aggimāla, and Dadhimāla oceans.
